recent_commits.message: Show the specific reason for each flagged data-quality issue, not just a bare column name
recent_commits.body:
Every fold-out line in the Data Quality section previously showed only the
column and file name (e.g. "Ignore in Study S4a Data.csv"), with no
indication of what was actually wrong -- unreadable for checks like "Numeric
as text" where the reason varies per column. Each line now includes the
check's own detail message (data_check's findings$detail), and the generic
PII explanation table is removed since every PII line now states its own
specific match reason.

Also drops codebook_check's misalignment paragraph, which restated the same
"N variables, M% matched" numbers already given in the first bullet and then
guessed a single cause (computed scores/subscales) that does not fit every
mismatch -- e.g. a codebook naming columns by position (var1, var2, ...)
instead of by their real name. Replaced with a fold-out pairing each data
file's own column names against its own codebook's variable names and
labels, so the reader can see the actual mismatch directly.

recent_commits.message: Add the ResearchBox app: paste a link, get a condensed check report
recent_commits.body:
A minimal Shiny app for repository-only checks (repo_check, code_check,
data_check, codebook_check) against a single ResearchBox link, without
needing a manuscript upload. The report is condensed rather than the full
report() output: counts per issue type, each with a fold-out listing the
specific files/columns responsible, so the top-level view stays short but
nothing is hidden.

Also scrubs a code file's text to valid UTF-8 before regex-matching it for
data-file references (data_check_helpers.R): a script saved in a legacy
encoding (e.g. a Stata .do file) otherwise makes PCRE warn and silently
skip the match.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Sonnet 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

recent_commits.message: Fix Dryad zip-peek auth, multi-sheet Excel detection, and code-in-zip discovery
recent_commits.body:
Four issues found and fixed while validating metacheck against Cooper et
al.'s BES-corpus coding:

- #378/#380: zip_peek() and .remote_size()/.remote_content_length() made
  unauthenticated requests, which Dryad 401s on for any byte-touching
  endpoint. Both now route through the existing .auth_for_url() dispatcher
  instead of requiring each caller to opt in per host.

- #379: data_check's tabular-usability check only ever read the first
  sheet of a multi-sheet Excel workbook. When sheet 1 is a cover/metadata
  page (a common convention), a later sheet holding real tabular data was
  never inspected. data_read_head() now accepts a sheet argument, and
  data_check tries each remaining sheet before giving up on the file.

- #383: code_check() could not see code files inside a zip in three
  compounding ways -- it never read data_check's already-expanded
  structure, it had no zip-peek of its own, and the zip-expansion helper
  (.archive_rows()) discarded code-typed files outright. All three are
  fixed: code_check() prefers data_check's structure when available, gets
  its own zip-peek fallback (.code_expand_zip()), and .archive_rows() now
  keeps code alongside data/documentation.

Also carries the archive_url/archive_member wiring repo_check's zip-peek
expansion always intended (see its own prior comment) so a discovered
member's bytes, not just its name, can be fetched via a byte-range
request against the parent archive -- verified working in every isolated
test, but not yet confirmed reliable end-to-end in the full pipeline
(see #384).

Also fixes data_check's "no readable tabular data" early return silently
omitting structure/previews/gated_repos/manifest_path/group_no_evidence
from its result, which the above fixes depend on being present.

Closes #378, #379, #380, #383

recent_commits.message: Raise Dryad zip-vs-file threshold from 4 to 12 files
recent_commits.body:
Even at the original threshold of 4, the ZIP BUCKET'S HOURLY CAP
(20/hour -- separate from, and much tighter than, the 100/day ceiling)
was still being tripped repeatedly. Confirmed live against the real
Cooper-validation corpus run: batch 29 hit the same 5-file dataset's
zip request on three consecutive restarts, because restarting the
script does not reset the host's quota clock -- only real elapsed time
does, and not enough had passed between attempts.

Recomputed against the corpus data on disk at the time (873 Dryad
datasets): threshold 4 needs 190 zip requests corpus-wide, a 9.5/hour
average even under the best-case 2-day spread -- already exceeding the
20/hour ceiling on average, before accounting for a real run's uneven,
bursty pacing. Threshold 12 needs only 33 zip requests corpus-wide
(1.6/hour average), a far larger safety margin against the hourly wall
specifically.

This trades away some of the daily-quota-optimality the original
threshold-sweep found (12 is not that sweep's minimum-day threshold,
3-6 was) for practical hourly headroom that matters more once a real
run is actually hitting the hourly cap repeatedly.

Updated the "still uses zip" unit test from 8 to 16 files to stay above
the new threshold. Full file-level test-repo-download.R suite passes
clean (FAIL 0 | WARN 0 | SKIP 1 | PASS 77).
recent_commits.author: Lakens

recent_commits.message: Make Dryad's zip-vs-file-by-file download choice quota-aware
recent_commits.body:
Dryad throttles zip downloads and per-file downloads through two
independent per-IP quota buckets with very different sizes (confirmed
2026-09-01 against Dryad's own open-source rate-limit config,
datadryad/dryad-app config/initializers/rack_attack.rb +
config/app_config.yml): zip_downloads_per_day = 100,
file_downloads_per_day = 500 -- 5x more headroom on the file bucket.

The existing zip-vs-file decision only weighed request-count efficiency
(worth_it <- n_wanted > 50 || record_n <= 2*n_wanted), which picks zip
for nearly every real dataset since callers almost always want "all of
it". That means every Dryad dataset routed through the strict 100/day
zip bucket while the much larger 500/day file bucket sat unused.

Recomputed against the real Cooper-validation corpus (768 Dryad
datasets, 2710 files, 26 completed batches): always-zip needs 8
calendar days minimum (768 requests / 100 per day); always-file needs
6 (2710 / 500); routing small datasets (<=4 files) to the file bucket
and only larger ones to the zip bucket needs 3 -- the minimum across
every threshold from 0-50 tested, because it's the point where both
buckets fill up on the same day instead of one sitting idle while the
other alone is the bottleneck.

Added a `quota_worth_it <- n_wanted > 4L` gate ANDed onto the existing
request-count check, Dryad-only. Not applied to OSF/Zenodo/Dataverse/
GitHub/GitLab's identical-looking worth_it lines elsewhere in the same
file -- only Dryad's independent-stacked-throttle asymmetry has been
confirmed; changing the shared logic for hosts whose rate-limit
behaviour was never verified would be a separate, unjustified change.

Two new unit tests confirm a small Dryad dataset skips zip even though
the old request-count-only logic would have picked it, and a larger
one still uses zip. Full package test suite passes clean
(FAIL 0 | WARN 0 | SKIP 68 | PASS 4327).

recent_commits.message: Fix code_check crash when every file in a batch fails to download
recent_commits.body:
Three related bugs in code_check.R, all triggered by the same real-world
condition: every code file for a paper fails to download (e.g. a Dryad
rate limit genuinely exhausted mid-corpus-run), leaving code_files with
no rows that ever reached the per-file try block, so several columns are
absent entirely rather than NA-filled.

1. `sapply(code_files$library_max_between > 3, isTRUE)` on a zero-length
   input silently returns list() instead of logical(0). Subscripting
   code_files$file_name with that list() throws "invalid subscript type
   'list'" -- this is what actually crashed batch 27 of the Cooper
   validation corpus run. Fixed with vapply(), whose declared FUN.VALUE
   always returns the right type regardless of input length.

2. The comments-table block assumed `percentage_comment` always exists as
   a column and threw "undefined columns selected" when it didn't. Now
   guarded the same way n_analysed/comment_issue already handled it
   (treat an absent column as nothing to report).

3. The final summary_table `dplyr::summarise()` referenced code_abs_path,
   loaded_files_missing, percentage_comment, and parse_error unguarded.
   code_setwd already had an `if (col %in% names(code_files))` guard for
   the same reason; the other four did not. Added the same guard to all
   of them via a small has_col() helper.

Reproduced deterministically with a mocked download_repo_files() that
always fails, added as a regression test. Full package test suite passes
clean (FAIL 0 | WARN 0 | SKIP 68 | PASS 4323).

recent_commits.message: Wait for the real rate-limit reset instead of blind exponential backoff
recent_commits.body:
Found while investigating a code_check crash in a real 1861-paper corpus
run: Dryad's file-download endpoint sends IETF-draft RateLimit-Limit/
RateLimit-Remaining/RateLimit-Reset headers on a 429 -- confirmed live,
the limit is 100 requests/hour, reset on a fixed clock-hour boundary, and
NOT raised by OAuth authentication (despite this session's earlier
dryad_auth() work assuming it would be). The existing .storage_backoff()
only recognises the older Retry-After header, which Dryad never sends at
all, so every retry did blind exponential backoff (2s/4s/8s.../30s cap)
against a bucket that was provably empty until the next hour -- repeatedly
re-triggering the same wasted retry storm for every file in every affected
dataset, and very likely a major contributing factor to the heavy-429
conditions that preceded the crash.

The same header family (or the older X-RateLimit-* convention) is
confirmed live on Zenodo, GitHub, and GitLab too -- all four backends this
session has touched -- so this is built as shared logic across every
download call site, not a Dryad-specific patch. OSF/Figshare/Dataverse do
not expose it on the endpoints checked and are unaffected either way.

- .rate_limit_wait(): reads either header family off a 429 response,
  returns the real wait in seconds or NA if unconfirmed/absent.
- .storage_retry_after_factory() / .storage_is_transient_factory(): wired
  into req_retry()'s after/is_transient at every per-file download call
  site (.download_one(), .download_many_parallel()), so a
  confirmed-exhausted 429 waits for the REAL reset instead of blind
  backoff.
- .download_zip_to_cache() (the whole-dataset zip path) gains its own
  rate-limit check too: previously a 429's small error-page body would
  reach the streaming loop and either fail unzip() with a confusing
  "not a zip file" error or (worse) get silently treated as if it were
  real archive bytes. Now checks the status explicitly and waits for a
  confirmed reset (one retry) before falling through to the caller's
  file-by-file fallback.
- req_retry()'s own waits are completely silent by default -- a
  multi-minute-to-hour-long wait with zero console output looks identical
  to a hung process. A message() now announces any wait over 5 seconds,
  with the exact duration and how to skip it.
- New skip_on_api_limit parameter on download_repo_files() (default
  FALSE, i.e. always wait for the real reset -- explicit decision: the
  goal is completeness, not speed, for an unattended corpus build). TRUE
  gives up on a confirmed-exhausted request immediately instead, recorded
  in the failed attribute with an "API rate limit exhausted: "-prefixed
  message, filterable from every other kind of failure, so a caller can
  retry those specific files later once the quota has reset.

8 new unit tests in test-repo-download.R (1 skipped: an httr2
local_mocked_responses()/req_retry() interaction confirmed to behave
unreliably specifically under full-suite test ordering, not a bug in the
fix -- covered instead by an adjacent test using the more reliable
local_mocked_bindings() mock path; see that test's own comment). Full
package suite otherwise unaffected: FAIL 0 | WARN 0 | SKIP 68 | PASS 4314.

recent_commits.message: Support Figshare project URLs; surface unresolvable private share links
recent_commits.body:
Found while checking metacheck's output against Cooper et al.'s corpus:
an interim comparison run on the first 250 papers found 6 where Cooper
coded a real Figshare-hosted dataset but metacheck detected no repository
at all. Traced to two unsupported Figshare URL shapes -- neither a general
Figshare failure, since plain article/DOI links already worked correctly.

1. Project URLs (figshare.com/projects/<name>/<id>)

   A project bundles multiple articles rather than being one, so it has
   no article id of its own -- .figshare_id() correctly returned NA for
   it, but nothing then tried to resolve it as a project. Added
   .figshare_project_id() (extracts the trailing numeric id) and
   .figshare_project_articles() (lists the project's article ids via the
   public, unauthenticated GET /v2/projects/{id}/articles endpoint),
   wired into figshare_info() so a project url expands into one row per
   article -- the same shape as if the paper had cited each article url
   directly. Verified live against a real project (PERICLES Heritage
   values, 8 articles): repo_check() on the affected paper now finds 94
   files, up from 0.

   Also extended figshare_links()'s bare-text regex to match /projects/
   urls at all (it previously only matched articles/ndownloader), since
   both of the two real project-url misses in the sample were bare text
   mentions rather than real hyperlinks.

2. Private share links (figshare.com/s/<hash>)

   The hash is an opaque token with no article id anywhere in the URL,
   and Figshare's own resolution page sits behind an AWS WAF bot
   challenge -- confirmed live: a plain request gets an explicit "we
   need to verify you're not a robot... this requires JavaScript"
   challenge page, on every URL variant tried (the bare share link, one
   with a file= query parameter, and the direct ndownloader endpoint
   with a private_link= parameter, all three revealed by following a
   real browser's redirect chain). No documented plain-HTTP API
   alternative exists for a third party to resolve someone else's share
   link (the /v2/account/articles/{id}/private_links/ family is for the
   owner managing their own links). Passing the challenge programmatically
   would require emulating a real browser session, which is out of scope
   as bot-detection evasion.

   Rather than staying invisible (previously indistinguishable from "no
   Figshare link found"), figshare_links() now flags these via a new
   figshare_unsupported column, and repo_check() surfaces them through
   repo_error ("private share link cannot be resolved without a
   browser") -- the same mechanism already used for a private OSF
   project or a gated repository, so the link is visible in gated_repos
   for a human to follow up on manually.

Added tests/testthat/test-archive-figshare.R (28 assertions), since
Figshare previously had no dedicated test file at all.

- test-archive-osf-helpers.R: the osf_pat test's expect_no_error(help(...))

  in archive-osf-helpers.R, NAMESPACE, or man/ changed this session). 118

recent_commits.message: Fix Dryad whole-dataset zip download and add a real byte-cap during zip streaming
recent_commits.body:
download_repo_files() already had a Dryad zip-download branch (using the
stash:download bulk endpoint) that was supposed to replace N per-file
requests with one archive request, but it was silently dead code for the
entire Cooper corpus: the eligibility check matched repo_url against
"datadryad.org" only, while every real repo_url in the corpus is the
doi.org citation form (e.g. https://doi.org/10.5061/dryad.8sf7m0cjc) --
file_url (the per-file link) is datadryad.org, but repo_url never is. Every
Dryad dataset therefore fell through to file-by-file downloads (2 + N
requests each), which is what was driving the HTTP 429s seen at corpus
scale, independent of authentication.

Fixes, all verified live against real Dryad datasets from the corpus:

- Zip-eligibility regex now also matches the doi.org/10.5061/dryad form.
- .remote_content_length() gains a req_func parameter so its HEAD probe can
  be authenticated -- needed because Dryad requires a token for ANY call
  touching file bytes, including HEAD, unlike every other backend this
  function probes.
- Dryad's bulk endpoint still can't report its size via either method (HEAD
  answers 403 InvalidSignatureException -- its pre-signed S3 URL's
  signature is verb-specific; GET is chunked with no Content-Length at
  all), so the zip-vs-file-by-file size gate now falls back to summing the
  file sizes repo_check() already listed as a conservative estimate,
  rather than always failing "unknown size" and disabling the zip path
  permanently for this backend.
- .download_zip_to_cache() rewritten to stream via req_perform_connection()
  (req_perform_stream() is deprecated as of httr2 1.2.0) with a real
  max_bytes cap enforced DURING the download and a manual wall-clock
  timeout to replace the one req_timeout() no longer provides in this mode.
  Wired max_download_size through to it for OSF/Zenodo/Dataverse/Dryad
  (not GitHub/GitLab, whose zip transport is deliberately unbounded by
  design). This closes metacheck issue #366's second bug: a zip fallback
  with only a wall-clock timeout can still pull many GB on a fast
  connection before timing out (the issue's own example: 2.47GB for one
  failed text file on OSF).

Verified end-to-end against doi:10.5061/dryad.8sf7m0cjc: the fix correctly
downloads all 3 files as one zip request instead of 3+2, and a deliberately
tiny max_bytes correctly aborts the stream with zero files extracted.

Adds a full GitLab.com backend (archive-gitlab.R), matching the shape of
the existing GitHub backend: link detection (gitlab.com URLs and bare
"owner/repo" mentions near "gitlab"), repo path parsing, a paginated
file-tree listing (GitLab's tree endpoint caps at 100 entries/page, unlike
GitHub's single-request Git Trees API), file-size backfill via a batched
GraphQL repository.blobs(paths:) query (the REST tree listing has no size
field), licence detection, and complete-repository download via GitLab's
archive.zip endpoint (wired into repo-download.R the same way GitHub's
zipball is, since neither supports HTTP Range requests for a zip_peek()-
style partial read).

Separately, surfaces doi/license metadata in repo_check()'s new
repo_metadata field (one row per repository, not per paper -- a paper can
link more than one repository with different licences) for every backend
that already fetches this as part of a request it makes anyway: Dryad,
Zenodo, Dataverse, Figshare, ReShare, GitHub, GitLab, and PsychArchives
(the last via a new "doi" attribute on psycharchives_file_download(),
alongside its existing "rights" attribute). Previously this data was
fetched and then discarded before reaching the module's output. OSF's
licence is included too, but gated behind a new osf_license parameter
(default FALSE) since OSF requires one genuinely additional API request
per project that this module would not otherwise make, unlike every other
backend above.

Four real bugs were found and fixed while verifying this against live
GitLab.com repositories:
- New GitLab functions were tagged @export but NAMESPACE was never
  regenerated, so none of them were actually callable.
- httr2::req_url_query() silently breaks (404) when the request path
  already contains a percent-encoded segment (GitLab's "namespace%2Fproject"
  project id) -- fixed by building query strings directly into the URL.
- c() on a named list of named vectors prefixes each inner name with the
  outer list's name ("1..dockerignore" instead of ".dockerignore"),
  silently corrupting the path->size lookup in .gitlab_blob_sizes() even
  though the underlying GraphQL data was correct -- fixed with unname().
- GitLab's GraphQL API enforces a query-complexity budget (default max
  200); a blobs(paths:) query with 100 paths costs 212 and fails outright
  (HTTP 200 with an error in the body, not an HTTP error status, so this
  failed silently). Empirically confirmed the real cutoff is 94 paths;
  batch size reduced from 100 to 90 for margin.

Verified live against gitlab-org/gitlab-runner (1432 files, full
pagination, all files with backfilled sizes, licence "mit" correctly
detected) and end-to-end through repo_check() (table/summary_table/
repo_metadata all correctly populated). Cross-checked that Dryad's
repo_metadata (real doi + CC0 licence) and other existing backends are
unaffected.

recent_commits.message: Add Dryad OAuth2 client-credentials auth (resolves #370)
recent_commits.body:
dryad_pat() only accepts a single, manually-obtained OAuth2 bearer token,
which Dryad issues with a 10-hour lifetime. Any corpus run longer than 10
hours (or any interactive session spanning a coffee break) needed the
token manually regenerated and re-set mid-run, since .dryad_headers()
just attached whatever static string dryad_pat() currently held.

Dryad also issues a client id/secret pair, meant for the OAuth2
client-credentials grant (POST https://datadryad.org/oauth/token) --
trading those credentials for a short-lived access token that gets
refreshed automatically for as long as the credentials stay valid, with
no manual re-entry.

Adds dryad_auth(client_id, client_secret), parallel to dryad_pat(), that
stores the credentials (also readable from DRYAD_CLIENT_ID/
DRYAD_CLIENT_SECRET environment variables, the same way dryad_pat() reads
DRYAD_PAT) and builds an httr2::oauth_client(). .dryad_headers() now uses
httr2::req_oauth_client_credentials() when a client is set -- which
handles the whole token fetch/cache/automatic-refresh cycle transparently
-- falling back to the existing static dryad_pat() bearer header when
only a raw token is available.

Verified live: dryad_auth() correctly read real client credentials from
the environment, and dryad_file_download() against a real Dryad dataset
downloaded all 3 files successfully with checksums verified, confirming
the token exchange works end-to-end for actual file downloads (not just
metadata/listing calls, which never required a token).

recent_commits.message: Attach paper_id to naming_issues; fix empty-result schema loss on batch runs
recent_commits.body:
Two related follow-ups to the per-paper summary_table fix (d53090b),
both found while testing a batched multi-paper corpus run:

repo_check: the module's returned naming_issues field was still the
corpus-wide, unattributed table (keyed only by file_name), not the
paper_id-tagged version already built for the per-paper summary_table
count. data_check() reads this field via get_prev_outputs("repo_check",
"naming_issues") for its own per-file "Naming issue" column, so on a
multi-paper run it could not tell which paper a naming issue belonged to.
Fixed by returning the already-built, paper_id-tagged table instead of
the untagged one. Also fixed a related bug this surfaced in
codebook_check.R: its empty-result path computed a fallback paper_id set
from unique(structure_df$paper_id), which breaks when structure_df is a
real but zero-row data frame (character(0), not "no such column") --
this now falls through to .pid() correctly in that case too, instead of
producing a data.frame() row-count mismatch error.

code_check/codebook_check/data_check: each has an early-return path for
"nothing found" (no relevant code files; no extracted data columns; no
files at all) that returned either no `table` field at all or a bare,
schema-less data.frame(). Confirmed on a real 2-paper test batch where
neither paper had any code file: code_check's table came back with ZERO
columns instead of the normal paper_id/file_location/language/... schema.
On a corpus or batch run, even one paper hitting this path could silently
drop columns (or fill them with NA) for every other paper once combined
with bind_rows(). Each now returns its already-available, correctly-typed
but zero-row base frame instead.

Verified against test-module-repo_check.R, test-module-codebook_check.R,
and test-codebook-helpers.R (all pass), plus live reproductions of both
original bugs on real papers.

recent_commits.message: Fix per-paper summary_table aggregation when a module runs on a paperlist
recent_commits.body:
repo_check, data_check, and codebook_check each computed part of their
summary_table using a corpus-wide scalar instead of a per-paper count when
run once on a whole paperlist (module_run()'s normal calling convention for
a corpus). Confirmed on a real 1857-paper run:

- repo_check: files_unknown and naming_issues were the same two numbers on
  every paper's row (a total across every paper, not that paper's own
  count).
- data_check: summary_table (and its spreadsheet-validation half,
  dv_summary_table) collapsed to a single row tagged with only the first
  paper's id, so every other paper's data_file_n/column_n/empty_col_n
  showed 0 or NA regardless of what that paper's repository actually
  contained.
- codebook_check: the same collapse-to-one-id pattern in its summary_table,
  plus a related but more serious bug in match_column_labels() and its two
  LLM-driven matching tiers: matching was keyed on normalised column name
  only, with no paper_id constraint, so a column named e.g. "age" in one
  paper could match a different paper's codebook variable of the same
  name. Also fixed two rules-based scale/task detectors
  (.identify_scales_rules, .identify_tasks_rules) that silently skipped
  manuscript-text corroboration on every paperlist run (including the
  default llm_use(FALSE) path), since their own paper-detection guard was
  never true for a paperlist.

All three modules now compute per-paper counts via proper paper_id
grouping/joins instead of ungrouped scalars, matching the pattern already
used correctly in code_check.R and stat_p_exact.R. codebook_vars_df also
gained a paper_id column (stamped at the point each codebook/README/haven
file is parsed) so its own per-paper aggregation and the paper-scoped
match in match_column_labels() have something to key on;
match_column_labels() falls back to its original unscoped behaviour when
codebook_vars_df has no paper_id column at all, for callers that construct
it directly (as three existing unit tests do).

Verified against test-module-repo_check.R, test-module-codebook_check.R,
and test-codebook-helpers.R (all pass), plus live multi-paper runs
confirming each fixed module now produces correct, distinct per-paper
values.

only accepts one (files = NULL). This crashed data_check() with

cleanly.

sits at line 5 and the first mislabelled section at line 102, so a reader arriving by
anchor, by git diff, by a PyPI render or by a search hit lands ON the section with

reader who starts at the top, which is the one reader who least needs it.

with the re-scoped 2026-08-27 consult block, which is a record about work in progress
and now sits literally where it belongs:

  - A repeated line is furniture because of WHERE ON THE PAGE it sits
  - The page boundaries had to come back first — five steps were destroying them
  - Delete furniture, never data — the strip now actually consults the guard

KEPT under `## [2.4.138]`: `changes_made` counts minus signs by contract — the one
section of the four that the signal table shows actually shipped (changes_made_by_step
4 on main against 5 in the tree).

Why it matters beyond tidiness: this is a public repo and a PyPI package. A researcher
who installs 2.4.138 and reads its notes would have believed they got the
page-distribution gate and the page-boundary restoration. They did not. That is this
project's "no pretending" rule exactly — do not document a capability the code does not
perform — and it is the same class as the defect the block itself was written about.

THE MOVE IS PROVEN WHOLESALE, NOT A REWRITE. The sections were relocated by slicing and

`_normalize_text` stripped standalone page numbers with

consume the page boundary standing beside the number it was deleting. It had been
wrong since it was written, and a running footer sitting between the two held it
latent. The moment anything stripped that footer, every form feed in the document
went with it -- and with them the `\n\f\f\n` marker that separates the footnote
appendix, folding it back into the body where a consumer reads it as running text.

Two papers in the render baseline were ALREADY in that state at HEAD: they report

carries no appendix at all. Nothing had ever noticed, because nothing compared
the two.

    papers gaining page breaks           16   (+1 to +17 each)
    footnote appendices RESTORED          2   (0 -> 1,288 and 0 -> 2,165 bytes)
    papers made worse on any metric        0

test pins THE SHIPPED RULE rather than a retyped copy of the pattern. The form
feed is CAPTURED and put back, not merely excluded from the class: a page number
is often the first thing on a new page, so the line itself begins with the break,
and excluding it stopped those lines matching at all ('496'..'502' reappeared in
the body of 10.1016/j.jesp.2009.12.010). `_drop()` in F0's strip loop keeps the

highlights.message: Show the specific reason for each flagged data-quality issue, not just a bare column name
highlights.body:
Every fold-out line in the Data Quality section previously showed only the
column and file name (e.g. "Ignore in Study S4a Data.csv"), with no
indication of what was actually wrong -- unreadable for checks like "Numeric
as text" where the reason varies per column. Each line now includes the
check's own detail message (data_check's findings$detail), and the generic
PII explanation table is removed since every PII line now states its own
specific match reason.

Also drops codebook_check's misalignment paragraph, which restated the same
"N variables, M% matched" numbers already given in the first bullet and then
guessed a single cause (computed scores/subscales) that does not fit every
mismatch -- e.g. a codebook naming columns by position (var1, var2, ...)
instead of by their real name. Replaced with a fold-out pairing each data
file's own column names against its own codebook's variable names and
labels, so the reader can see the actual mismatch directly.

highlights.message: Fix Dryad zip-peek auth, multi-sheet Excel detection, and code-in-zip discovery
highlights.body:
Four issues found and fixed while validating metacheck against Cooper et
al.'s BES-corpus coding:

- #378/#380: zip_peek() and .remote_size()/.remote_content_length() made
  unauthenticated requests, which Dryad 401s on for any byte-touching
  endpoint. Both now route through the existing .auth_for_url() dispatcher
  instead of requiring each caller to opt in per host.

- #379: data_check's tabular-usability check only ever read the first
  sheet of a multi-sheet Excel workbook. When sheet 1 is a cover/metadata
  page (a common convention), a later sheet holding real tabular data was
  never inspected. data_read_head() now accepts a sheet argument, and
  data_check tries each remaining sheet before giving up on the file.

- #383: code_check() could not see code files inside a zip in three
  compounding ways -- it never read data_check's already-expanded
  structure, it had no zip-peek of its own, and the zip-expansion helper
  (.archive_rows()) discarded code-typed files outright. All three are
  fixed: code_check() prefers data_check's structure when available, gets
  its own zip-peek fallback (.code_expand_zip()), and .archive_rows() now
  keeps code alongside data/documentation.

Also carries the archive_url/archive_member wiring repo_check's zip-peek
expansion always intended (see its own prior comment) so a discovered
member's bytes, not just its name, can be fetched via a byte-range
request against the parent archive -- verified working in every isolated
test, but not yet confirmed reliable end-to-end in the full pipeline
(see #384).

Also fixes data_check's "no readable tabular data" early return silently
omitting structure/previews/gated_repos/manifest_path/group_no_evidence
from its result, which the above fixes depend on being present.

Closes #378, #379, #380, #383

Found by articlerepository-c0 in a 2.4.126 render-baseline; the load-bearing question -- "does CURRENT docpluck still do this?" -- was filed COULD-NOT-VERIFY. It does. rendered bytes 59703 · NUL count 22 CONTROL, same code path, 10.5465/annals.2016.0011 : NUL count 0 p2 Table 1 prints Cramer's V = 0.067 [-0.108, 0.218] <- SPANS zero docpluck emits [ 0.108, 0.218] <- reads as EXCLUDING zero p4 Table 2 "Comparison of differences across conditions" prints Tversky & Shafir, 1992 (between-subjects) 199 -1 -31 -30 213 14 31 17 docpluck emits the three SIGNED values as 1 / 31 / 30 and the three unsigned values intact. The row carries its own two-sided control. All 22 NULs were checked against the page; every one sits where the paper prints a minus. pdftotext recovers the glyph as U+2212, and docpluck's own BODY-TEXT channel gets it right -- the same document renders "[- 0.108," in prose and "[ 0.108," in the table. One document, two channels, two different published values. ROOT CAUSE -- THE REPAIR EXISTS AND CANNOT FIRE. cell_cleaning.py:113-118 already carries it, and its comment names this exact case ('"(cid:0) 31" is -31'): _html_escape("(cid:0) 31") -> "-31" works _html_escape("\x00 31") -> "\x00 31" does nothing Asked of Camelot directly (page 4, flavor=stream): 21 raw cells carry a NUL and NONE carries "(cid:0)". Camelot emits the raw NUL on this path. The older pdfminer-based spike baseline DID emit "(cid:0)", which is presumably why the repair was written that way and why it has looked correct ever since. It is a repair aimed at a representation that no longer arrives. PINNED, NOT FIXED. Five strict xfails; two controls pass. strict=True means a fix turns them XPASS, which pytest reports as a FAILURE -- so the defect cannot be fixed without updating this file. A record of a known defect, not a weakened gate. Not fixed in this commit for one reason, and it is not scope: a fix CHANGES SIGNS in the table channel, a full Camelot suite was already running on a frozen tree, and there is an 08:00 convergence stop. Landing a sign-changing edit that cannot be verified by a full run is the "a fix can be worse than the defect" shape. THE TRAP THE FIX MUST CLEAR, measured and pinned by the last test here: \x00 is ALSO docpluck's own fold sentinel (_MERGE_SEPARATOR = "\x00BR\x00"). A folded header can put a DIGIT right after the closing NUL -- _html_escape("Replication\x00BR\x0095% CI") -> "Replication
95% CI" -- so a naive \x00-before-digit repair inside _html_escape would destroy the fold AND inject a minus that was never printed, turning a data-loss defect into a data-fabrication one. highlights.body:

script under tools/ or scripts/ has no route to the repo root and a bare
`import docpluck` silently resolves to whatever is installed.

Measured 2026-09-01 on this tree, three arms:

    python tools/<probe>.py         -> site-packages\docpluck  2.4.137
    python -c "import docpluck"     -> <repo>\docpluck         2.4.138
    python <probe-at-repo-root>.py  -> <repo>\docpluck         2.4.138

The third arm is the control: it isolates the cause to the script's DIRECTORY
rather than to "running a script at all". Arm two is structurally incapable of
showing the defect, which is why it survived -- the obvious check measures a
different thing.

Census of all 34 docpluck importers under tools/ + scripts/: 16 resolved the
installed 2.4.137, INCLUDING scripts/verify_corpus.py, the 26-paper baseline
that gates every iterate cycle. A fix could be verified all night against a
library it had not touched, with every log line naming the tree.

-- while the same defect sat in fifteen others.

tools/*.py needs 1 and tools/diag/*.py needs 2, so a count encodes the file's
current location into its correctness and silently regresses the moment a file
moves -- regresses in the direction that resolves site-packages again.

red first. It runs each script for real under runpy with sys.path[0] set to the
script's own directory and halts at the moment docpluck is imported.

unclosed; extending the block ran on into argparse; an empty argparse Namespace

caught only because the test scores a failed MEASUREMENT as a failure, never as
a pass -- a skip, an N/A and an indeterminate are all green-shaped and none of
them is a measurement.

highlights.body:
Even at the original threshold of 4, the ZIP BUCKET'S HOURLY CAP
(20/hour -- separate from, and much tighter than, the 100/day ceiling)
was still being tripped repeatedly. Confirmed live against the real
Cooper-validation corpus run: batch 29 hit the same 5-file dataset's
zip request on three consecutive restarts, because restarting the
script does not reset the host's quota clock -- only real elapsed time
does, and not enough had passed between attempts.

Recomputed against the corpus data on disk at the time (873 Dryad
datasets): threshold 4 needs 190 zip requests corpus-wide, a 9.5/hour
average even under the best-case 2-day spread -- already exceeding the
20/hour ceiling on average, before accounting for a real run's uneven,
bursty pacing. Threshold 12 needs only 33 zip requests corpus-wide
(1.6/hour average), a far larger safety margin against the hourly wall
specifically.

This trades away some of the daily-quota-optimality the original
threshold-sweep found (12 is not that sweep's minimum-day threshold,
3-6 was) for practical hourly headroom that matters more once a real
run is actually hitting the hourly cap repeatedly.

the new threshold. Full file-level test-repo-download.R suite passes
clean (FAIL 0 | WARN 0 | SKIP 1 | PASS 77).

highlights.message: Make Dryad's zip-vs-file-by-file download choice quota-aware
highlights.body:
Dryad throttles zip downloads and per-file downloads through two
independent per-IP quota buckets with very different sizes (confirmed
2026-09-01 against Dryad's own open-source rate-limit config,
datadryad/dryad-app config/initializers/rack_attack.rb +
config/app_config.yml): zip_downloads_per_day = 100,
file_downloads_per_day = 500 -- 5x more headroom on the file bucket.

The existing zip-vs-file decision only weighed request-count efficiency
(worth_it <- n_wanted > 50 || record_n <= 2*n_wanted), which picks zip
for nearly every real dataset since callers almost always want "all of
it". That means every Dryad dataset routed through the strict 100/day
zip bucket while the much larger 500/day file bucket sat unused.

Recomputed against the real Cooper-validation corpus (768 Dryad
datasets, 2710 files, 26 completed batches): always-zip needs 8
calendar days minimum (768 requests / 100 per day); always-file needs
6 (2710 / 500); routing small datasets (<=4 files) to the file bucket
and only larger ones to the zip bucket needs 3 -- the minimum across
every threshold from 0-50 tested, because it's the point where both
buckets fill up on the same day instead of one sitting idle while the
other alone is the bottleneck.

Added a `quota_worth_it <- n_wanted > 4L` gate ANDed onto the existing
request-count check, Dryad-only. Not applied to OSF/Zenodo/Dataverse/
GitHub/GitLab's identical-looking worth_it lines elsewhere in the same
file -- only Dryad's independent-stacked-throttle asymmetry has been
confirmed; changing the shared logic for hosts whose rate-limit
behaviour was never verified would be a separate, unjustified change.

Two new unit tests confirm a small Dryad dataset skips zip even though
the old request-count-only logic would have picked it, and a larger
one still uses zip. Full package test suite passes clean
(FAIL 0 | WARN 0 | SKIP 68 | PASS 4327).

highlights.message: Wait for the real rate-limit reset instead of blind exponential backoff
highlights.body:
Found while investigating a code_check crash in a real 1861-paper corpus
run: Dryad's file-download endpoint sends IETF-draft RateLimit-Limit/
RateLimit-Remaining/RateLimit-Reset headers on a 429 -- confirmed live,
the limit is 100 requests/hour, reset on a fixed clock-hour boundary, and
NOT raised by OAuth authentication (despite this session's earlier
dryad_auth() work assuming it would be). The existing .storage_backoff()
only recognises the older Retry-After header, which Dryad never sends at
all, so every retry did blind exponential backoff (2s/4s/8s.../30s cap)
against a bucket that was provably empty until the next hour -- repeatedly
re-triggering the same wasted retry storm for every file in every affected
dataset, and very likely a major contributing factor to the heavy-429
conditions that preceded the crash.

The same header family (or the older X-RateLimit-* convention) is
confirmed live on Zenodo, GitHub, and GitLab too -- all four backends this
session has touched -- so this is built as shared logic across every
download call site, not a Dryad-specific patch. OSF/Figshare/Dataverse do
not expose it on the endpoints checked and are unaffected either way.

- .rate_limit_wait(): reads either header family off a 429 response,
  returns the real wait in seconds or NA if unconfirmed/absent.
- .storage_retry_after_factory() / .storage_is_transient_factory(): wired
  into req_retry()'s after/is_transient at every per-file download call
  site (.download_one(), .download_many_parallel()), so a
  confirmed-exhausted 429 waits for the REAL reset instead of blind
  backoff.
- .download_zip_to_cache() (the whole-dataset zip path) gains its own
  rate-limit check too: previously a 429's small error-page body would
  reach the streaming loop and either fail unzip() with a confusing
  "not a zip file" error or (worse) get silently treated as if it were
  real archive bytes. Now checks the status explicitly and waits for a
  confirmed reset (one retry) before falling through to the caller's
  file-by-file fallback.
- req_retry()'s own waits are completely silent by default -- a
  multi-minute-to-hour-long wait with zero console output looks identical
  to a hung process. A message() now announces any wait over 5 seconds,
  with the exact duration and how to skip it.
- New skip_on_api_limit parameter on download_repo_files() (default
  FALSE, i.e. always wait for the real reset -- explicit decision: the
  goal is completeness, not speed, for an unattended corpus build). TRUE
  gives up on a confirmed-exhausted request immediately instead, recorded
  in the failed attribute with an "API rate limit exhausted: "-prefixed
  message, filterable from every other kind of failure, so a caller can
  retry those specific files later once the quota has reset.

8 new unit tests in test-repo-download.R (1 skipped: an httr2
local_mocked_responses()/req_retry() interaction confirmed to behave
unreliably specifically under full-suite test ordering, not a bug in the
fix -- covered instead by an adjacent test using the more reliable
local_mocked_bindings() mock path; see that test's own comment). Full
package suite otherwise unaffected: FAIL 0 | WARN 0 | SKIP 68 | PASS 4314.

highlights.message: Support Figshare project URLs; surface unresolvable private share links
highlights.body:
Found while checking metacheck's output against Cooper et al.'s corpus:
an interim comparison run on the first 250 papers found 6 where Cooper
coded a real Figshare-hosted dataset but metacheck detected no repository
at all. Traced to two unsupported Figshare URL shapes -- neither a general
Figshare failure, since plain article/DOI links already worked correctly.

1. Project URLs (figshare.com/projects/<name>/<id>)

   A project bundles multiple articles rather than being one, so it has
   no article id of its own -- .figshare_id() correctly returned NA for
   it, but nothing then tried to resolve it as a project. Added
   .figshare_project_id() (extracts the trailing numeric id) and
   .figshare_project_articles() (lists the project's article ids via the
   public, unauthenticated GET /v2/projects/{id}/articles endpoint),
   wired into figshare_info() so a project url expands into one row per
   article -- the same shape as if the paper had cited each article url
   directly. Verified live against a real project (PERICLES Heritage
   values, 8 articles): repo_check() on the affected paper now finds 94
   files, up from 0.

   Also extended figshare_links()'s bare-text regex to match /projects/
   urls at all (it previously only matched articles/ndownloader), since
   both of the two real project-url misses in the sample were bare text
   mentions rather than real hyperlinks.

2. Private share links (figshare.com/s/<hash>)

   The hash is an opaque token with no article id anywhere in the URL,
   and Figshare's own resolution page sits behind an AWS WAF bot
   challenge -- confirmed live: a plain request gets an explicit "we
   need to verify you're not a robot... this requires JavaScript"
   challenge page, on every URL variant tried (the bare share link, one
   with a file= query parameter, and the direct ndownloader endpoint
   with a private_link= parameter, all three revealed by following a
   real browser's redirect chain). No documented plain-HTTP API
   alternative exists for a third party to resolve someone else's share
   link (the /v2/account/articles/{id}/private_links/ family is for the
   owner managing their own links). Passing the challenge programmatically
   would require emulating a real browser session, which is out of scope
   as bot-detection evasion.

   Rather than staying invisible (previously indistinguishable from "no
   Figshare link found"), figshare_links() now flags these via a new
   figshare_unsupported column, and repo_check() surfaces them through
   repo_error ("private share link cannot be resolved without a
   browser") -- the same mechanism already used for a private OSF
   project or a gated repository, so the link is visible in gated_repos
   for a human to follow up on manually.

Figshare previously had no dedicated test file at all.

highlights.message: Fix Dryad whole-dataset zip download and add a real byte-cap during zip streaming
highlights.body:
download_repo_files() already had a Dryad zip-download branch (using the
stash:download bulk endpoint) that was supposed to replace N per-file
requests with one archive request, but it was silently dead code for the
entire Cooper corpus: the eligibility check matched repo_url against
"datadryad.org" only, while every real repo_url in the corpus is the
doi.org citation form (e.g. https://doi.org/10.5061/dryad.8sf7m0cjc) --
file_url (the per-file link) is datadryad.org, but repo_url never is. Every
Dryad dataset therefore fell through to file-by-file downloads (2 + N
requests each), which is what was driving the HTTP 429s seen at corpus
scale, independent of authentication.

Fixes, all verified live against real Dryad datasets from the corpus:

- Zip-eligibility regex now also matches the doi.org/10.5061/dryad form.
- .remote_content_length() gains a req_func parameter so its HEAD probe can
  be authenticated -- needed because Dryad requires a token for ANY call
  touching file bytes, including HEAD, unlike every other backend this
  function probes.
- Dryad's bulk endpoint still can't report its size via either method (HEAD
  answers 403 InvalidSignatureException -- its pre-signed S3 URL's
  signature is verb-specific; GET is chunked with no Content-Length at
  all), so the zip-vs-file-by-file size gate now falls back to summing the
  file sizes repo_check() already listed as a conservative estimate,
  rather than always failing "unknown size" and disabling the zip path
  permanently for this backend.
- .download_zip_to_cache() rewritten to stream via req_perform_connection()
  (req_perform_stream() is deprecated as of httr2 1.2.0) with a real
  max_bytes cap enforced DURING the download and a manual wall-clock
  timeout to replace the one req_timeout() no longer provides in this mode.
  Wired max_download_size through to it for OSF/Zenodo/Dataverse/Dryad
  (not GitHub/GitLab, whose zip transport is deliberately unbounded by
  design). This closes metacheck issue #366's second bug: a zip fallback
  with only a wall-clock timeout can still pull many GB on a fast
  connection before timing out (the issue's own example: 2.47GB for one
  failed text file on OSF).

Verified end-to-end against doi:10.5061/dryad.8sf7m0cjc: the fix correctly
downloads all 3 files as one zip request instead of 3+2, and a deliberately
tiny max_bytes correctly aborts the stream with zero files extracted.

highlights.message: Add GitLab support and surface repository licence/DOI metadata
highlights.body:
Adds a full GitLab.com backend (archive-gitlab.R), matching the shape of
the existing GitHub backend: link detection (gitlab.com URLs and bare
"owner/repo" mentions near "gitlab"), repo path parsing, a paginated
file-tree listing (GitLab's tree endpoint caps at 100 entries/page, unlike
GitHub's single-request Git Trees API), file-size backfill via a batched
GraphQL repository.blobs(paths:) query (the REST tree listing has no size
field), licence detection, and complete-repository download via GitLab's
archive.zip endpoint (wired into repo-download.R the same way GitHub's
zipball is, since neither supports HTTP Range requests for a zip_peek()-
style partial read).

Separately, surfaces doi/license metadata in repo_check()'s new
repo_metadata field (one row per repository, not per paper -- a paper can
link more than one repository with different licences) for every backend
that already fetches this as part of a request it makes anyway: Dryad,
Zenodo, Dataverse, Figshare, ReShare, GitHub, GitLab, and PsychArchives
(the last via a new "doi" attribute on psycharchives_file_download(),
alongside its existing "rights" attribute). Previously this data was
fetched and then discarded before reaching the module's output. OSF's
licence is included too, but gated behind a new osf_license parameter
(default FALSE) since OSF requires one genuinely additional API request
per project that this module would not otherwise make, unlike every other
backend above.

Four real bugs were found and fixed while verifying this against live
GitLab.com repositories:
- New GitLab functions were tagged @export but NAMESPACE was never
  regenerated, so none of them were actually callable.
- httr2::req_url_query() silently breaks (404) when the request path
  already contains a percent-encoded segment (GitLab's "namespace%2Fproject"
  project id) -- fixed by building query strings directly into the URL.
- c() on a named list of named vectors prefixes each inner name with the
  outer list's name ("1..dockerignore" instead of ".dockerignore"),
  silently corrupting the path->size lookup in .gitlab_blob_sizes() even
  though the underlying GraphQL data was correct -- fixed with unname().
- GitLab's GraphQL API enforces a query-complexity budget (default max
  200); a blobs(paths:) query with 100 paths costs 212 and fails outright
  (HTTP 200 with an error in the body, not an HTTP error status, so this
  failed silently). Empirically confirmed the real cutoff is 94 paths;
  batch size reduced from 100 to 90 for margin.

Verified live against gitlab-org/gitlab-runner (1432 files, full
pagination, all files with backfilled sizes, licence "mit" correctly
detected) and end-to-end through repo_check() (table/summary_table/
repo_metadata all correctly populated). Cross-checked that Dryad's
repo_metadata (real doi + CC0 licence) and other existing backends are
unaffected.

highlights.message: Add Dryad OAuth2 client-credentials auth (resolves #370)
highlights.body:
dryad_pat() only accepts a single, manually-obtained OAuth2 bearer token,
which Dryad issues with a 10-hour lifetime. Any corpus run longer than 10
hours (or any interactive session spanning a coffee break) needed the
token manually regenerated and re-set mid-run, since .dryad_headers()
just attached whatever static string dryad_pat() currently held.

Dryad also issues a client id/secret pair, meant for the OAuth2
client-credentials grant (POST https://datadryad.org/oauth/token) --
trading those credentials for a short-lived access token that gets
refreshed automatically for as long as the credentials stay valid, with
no manual re-entry.

Adds dryad_auth(client_id, client_secret), parallel to dryad_pat(), that
stores the credentials (also readable from DRYAD_CLIENT_ID/
DRYAD_CLIENT_SECRET environment variables, the same way dryad_pat() reads
DRYAD_PAT) and builds an httr2::oauth_client(). .dryad_headers() now uses
httr2::req_oauth_client_credentials() when a client is set -- which
handles the whole token fetch/cache/automatic-refresh cycle transparently
-- falling back to the existing static dryad_pat() bearer header when
only a raw token is available.

Verified live: dryad_auth() correctly read real client credentials from
the environment, and dryad_file_download() against a real Dryad dataset
downloaded all 3 files successfully with checksums verified, confirming
the token exchange works end-to-end for actual file downloads (not just
metadata/listing calls, which never required a token).

highlights.message: Attach paper_id to naming_issues; fix empty-result schema loss on batch runs
highlights.body:
Two related follow-ups to the per-paper summary_table fix (d53090b),
both found while testing a batched multi-paper corpus run:

repo_check: the module's returned naming_issues field was still the
corpus-wide, unattributed table (keyed only by file_name), not the
paper_id-tagged version already built for the per-paper summary_table
count. data_check() reads this field via get_prev_outputs("repo_check",
"naming_issues") for its own per-file "Naming issue" column, so on a
multi-paper run it could not tell which paper a naming issue belonged to.
Fixed by returning the already-built, paper_id-tagged table instead of
the untagged one. Also fixed a related bug this surfaced in
codebook_check.R: its empty-result path computed a fallback paper_id set
from unique(structure_df$paper_id), which breaks when structure_df is a
real but zero-row data frame (character(0), not "no such column") --
this now falls through to .pid() correctly in that case too, instead of
producing a data.frame() row-count mismatch error.

code_check/codebook_check/data_check: each has an early-return path for
"nothing found" (no relevant code files; no extracted data columns; no
files at all) that returned either no `table` field at all or a bare,
schema-less data.frame(). Confirmed on a real 2-paper test batch where
neither paper had any code file: code_check's table came back with ZERO
columns instead of the normal paper_id/file_location/language/... schema.
On a corpus or batch run, even one paper hitting this path could silently
drop columns (or fill them with NA) for every other paper once combined
with bind_rows(). Each now returns its already-available, correctly-typed
but zero-row base frame instead.

Verified against test-module-repo_check.R, test-module-codebook_check.R,
and test-codebook-helpers.R (all pass), plus live reproductions of both
original bugs on real papers.

highlights.message: Fix per-paper summary_table aggregation when a module runs on a paperlist
highlights.body:
repo_check, data_check, and codebook_check each computed part of their
summary_table using a corpus-wide scalar instead of a per-paper count when
run once on a whole paperlist (module_run()'s normal calling convention for
a corpus). Confirmed on a real 1857-paper run:

- repo_check: files_unknown and naming_issues were the same two numbers on
  every paper's row (a total across every paper, not that paper's own
  count).
- data_check: summary_table (and its spreadsheet-validation half,
  dv_summary_table) collapsed to a single row tagged with only the first
  paper's id, so every other paper's data_file_n/column_n/empty_col_n
  showed 0 or NA regardless of what that paper's repository actually
  contained.
- codebook_check: the same collapse-to-one-id pattern in its summary_table,
  plus a related but more serious bug in match_column_labels() and its two
  LLM-driven matching tiers: matching was keyed on normalised column name
  only, with no paper_id constraint, so a column named e.g. "age" in one
  paper could match a different paper's codebook variable of the same
  name. Also fixed two rules-based scale/task detectors
  (.identify_scales_rules, .identify_tasks_rules) that silently skipped
  manuscript-text corroboration on every paperlist run (including the
  default llm_use(FALSE) path), since their own paper-detection guard was
  never true for a paperlist.

All three modules now compute per-paper counts via proper paper_id
grouping/joins instead of ungrouped scalars, matching the pattern already
used correctly in code_check.R and stat_p_exact.R. codebook_vars_df also
gained a paper_id column (stamped at the point each codebook/README/haven
file is parsed) so its own per-paper aggregation and the paper-scoped
match in match_column_labels() have something to key on;
match_column_labels() falls back to its original unscoped behaviour when
codebook_vars_df has no paper_id column at all, for callers that construct
it directly (as three existing unit tests do).

Verified against test-module-repo_check.R, test-module-codebook_check.R,
and test-codebook-helpers.R (all pass), plus live multi-paper runs
confirming each fixed module now produces correct, distinct per-paper
values.

highlights.message: Fix crash in data_check when a paper has no readable tabular data
highlights.body:
.pid(columns_df, structure_df) passed two arguments to .pid(), which
only accepts one (files = NULL). This crashed data_check() with
"unused argument (structure_df)" whenever the module reached its
"no readable tabular data files" fallback branch -- e.g. a paper whose
only data files are non-rectangular/merged-cell spreadsheets, or has no
tabular data at all. The correct one-argument form, .pid(columns_df),
was already used seven lines below in the same commit that introduced
this bug (21a6c28, 2026-08-11).

Verified: 7 of 8 real BES-corpus papers that previously crashed now run
cleanly.
